title: Coding taxonomy: Activities do not reveal automation effects
desc: Classifies development, maintenance, testing and application domains without supporting conclusions about AI productivity, value or displacement.

kps.k: The cluster contributes a taxonomy of coding activity, not evidence of AI’s effects on work.
kps.d: Table S15 in “Who is using AI to code? Global diffusion and impact of generative AI” groups software libraries into 19 high-level communities and lists the 10 most common libraries in each. Gemini 2.5 generated the community labels from library membership. This describes the software domains represented; it does not independently measure AI adoption or impact.

kps.k: The taxonomy distinguishes application domains from development, maintenance and testing workflows.
kps.d: The classification separates scientific computing, data analysis and specialised machine-learning tasks from web applications, backends, infrastructure, hardware and specialised science. It also identifies packaging, documentation, Git workflows, systems diagnostics and internal framework testing. Its practical analytical value lies in distinguishing types of coding activity rather than treating coding as a single uniform task; the supplied material does not show whether AI performs differently across these categories.

kps.k: The supplied excerpts cannot resolve debates about productivity, economic value or labour displacement.
kps.d: The coding-diffusion excerpts provide no adoption rates, productivity estimates, labour-market findings or recommendations. The experienced-open-source-developer productivity summary contains no substantive findings, while the GDPval material contains only package names and versions. Consequently, this cluster supplies neither competing empirical claims nor a basis for conclusions about AI’s economic effects; the publications’ titles cannot fill those evidence gaps.

vlens.an: The supplied academia-and-research evidence supports the proposition that this cluster classifies coding activities but does not establish automation effects. The substantive source describes 19 software-library communities whose labels were generated from their member libraries, so its evidence concerns a descriptive taxonomy spanning application domains and development, maintenance and testing workflows—not measured AI adoption, productivity, economic value or labour displacement. Internal variation is evidentiary rather than argumentative: the taxonomy source directly supports the proposition, while the experienced-open-source-developer productivity record contains no findings or quotations and is therefore indeterminate, not contrary evidence. Because these are curated sources, this assessment applies only to the supplied records and does not characterise academia or research generally.

vlens.an: The supplied legal-tech vendor source supports the cluster’s principal proposition only in a limited, evidentiary sense: its excerpts consist of software package names and version specifications and contain no substantive claims about AI productivity, economic value, adoption or labour displacement. It therefore provides no basis for inferring automation effects from the listed coding activities. There is no material internal variation to assess because the curated evidence contains only this single vendor source and no substantive argument; this should not be generalised to legal-tech vendors as a group.

elens.an: The usable 2025 evidence supports the proposition that the supplied material does not establish AI’s effects on productivity, economic value or labour displacement. The GDPval record specifically identifies its excerpts as package names and version specifications rather than substantive claims. The experienced-open-source-developer record is materially different: it has no description, findings, key points or quotations, so its position is indeterminate rather than affirmative support. Thus, the common basis is evidentiary insufficiency, but one source demonstrates that insufficiency from the character of the excerpts while the other simply lacks analysable content. Neither record challenges the taxonomy-versus-effects distinction, and no inference about broader 2025 views or prevalence is warranted from this curated pair.

The 2026 source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. Its evidence is a descriptive taxonomy: it groups software libraries into 19 communities and uses Gemini 2.5 to label those communities from their constituent libraries. This substantiates the proposition that the material distinguishes coding domains and workflows but does not itself establish AI adoption, productivity, economic value or labour displacement. The taxonomy spans application development, scientific computing, infrastructure, maintenance and testing, yet that breadth should not be mistaken for measured variation in AI’s effects across those activities. There is no material internal disagreement in the supplied period evidence because only one curated source is represented; its main qualification is methodological—the labels are AI-generated descriptions rather than independently validated impact categories.
